What flowerbed work includes

Most bed jobs are some mix of the following. You can book the whole thing or just the part you need.

Weeding & sprayingBeds pulled clean by hand and treated so the weeds stay gone longer than a weekend.
Fresh pine strawThe north Louisiana standard. It knits together on slopes instead of washing out, and it goes down fast over a big bed.
Fresh mulchWhere you want a darker, more finished edge — front beds, around roses, along walkways.
Trimming bushes & shrubsShaping overgrown foundation plantings back off the siding and windows.
PlantingPutting in the shrubs, perennials or color you’ve picked out.
Removing plantsTaking out what’s dead, overgrown, or in the wrong place — roots and all.
Laying sodNew turf over bare, patchy or torn-up ground. Hot, heavy work that goes a lot faster with a crew.

Not sure what your beds need? Send a couple of photos to Jase at 318-805-8288. We’ll tell you what we’d do, roughly what it costs, and whether it’s worth doing now or waiting for the season.

Laying sod

If the ground is bare — a patch that never took, ruts from a build, somewhere a tree used to be — we lay new sod over it. It is genuinely hard work in a Louisiana summer, which is most of the reason people call rather than do it themselves.

Tell us roughly how much ground you’re covering and we’ll quote it. The same visit can take in a driveway wash and a haul-off of whatever came out of the yard.

Why beds go downhill here

Long growing season, heavy summer rain and plenty of shade mean three things happen to a north Louisiana flowerbed:

  • Weeds outrun you. The season effectively runs most of the year, so a bed that was clean in April is unrecognizable by July.
  • The straw or mulch disappears. It breaks down, gets stepped on, and washes toward the low side of the yard after a hard rain. Beds end up thin and patchy with bare dirt showing through.
  • Shrubs swallow the house. Foundation plantings grow into the siding and over the windows, which traps moisture against the wall — and that’s exactly where mildew starts.

A cleanout plus fresh straw resets all three at once, and it’s the single cheapest thing you can do to change how a house looks from the street.

How it works

1. We look at the beds

Clean beds next to a mildewed wall look half-finished. Most customers have us wash the house, driveway and walkway in the same visit, and a lot of them add a haul-off for the limbs and junk that turn up once the beds are cleared.

Questions

Flowerbed questions we get asked

Pine straw or mulch — which should I use?

Pine straw is the north Louisiana default for good reason: it’s cheaper to cover a large bed with, it locks together so it doesn’t float away in a hard rain or wash off a slope, and it suits the pines and azaleas most yards around here already have. Mulch gives a darker, more formal look and holds moisture better, so it tends to win on smaller front beds you see up close. We’ll tell you which we’d use on your beds and why.

When is the best time to redo my beds?

Late winter to early spring, before everything leafs out, is the easiest time — you can actually see what you’re working with, and fresh straw or mulch is in place before the weeds start. Fall is the other good window. That said, a bed full of weeds in July still looks better cleaned out than left alone.

Do you haul off what you cut and pull?

Yes. Trimmings, pulled weeds and removed plants leave with us — it’s the same truck we use for junk removal and hauling.

Can you do the beds and wash the house in the same visit?

That’s the most common way we get booked. We’ll wash the house and driveway first so the rinse-off doesn’t land on fresh straw, then clean out and re-dress the beds. One trip, one estimate.

Do you handle jobs beyond flowerbeds?

Tell us what you have in mind. Beds, trimming, planting and cleanup are our bread and butter; for anything outside that, call or text and we’ll give you a straight answer about whether it’s something we take on.
